en: The *Buddhabhāṣita-Ānandamukha-nīgharidha-dhāraṇī-sūtra*,
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhayaśas of North India during the Northern Wei Dynasty.
Thus have I heard.
At one time, the Buddha was staying among the great groves of Vaiśālī at a monastery named Gandhakuṭi-vyūha.
He was together with a great assembly of thirty thousand bhikṣus.
At that time, the Buddha wished to relinquish his life;
he himself predicted that in three months he would enter parinirvāṇa.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana,
commanding him to go to the trichiliocosm and summon all those therein who belong to the lineage of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
"Furthermore, let all those who have set out in the Mahāyāna come to this assembly.
Maudgalyāyana immediately received these instructions;
he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, paid his respects, and departed.
Relying on his own merit, he took a single step and ascended to the summit of Mount Sumeru.
Empowered by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual authority, he sat down and reflected:
"By what samādhi can I cause the sound of my invitation to be heard throughout the trichiliocosm?"
At that moment, the samādhi manifested exactly as he had intended,
and his voice was heard throughout all the ten directions.
At that time, one million bhikṣus came together at the vihāra.
The worthy Śāriputra again formed this thought:
"I too shall enter samādhi,
desiring to know the locations of the bhikṣus within Jambudvīpa, whether they be far or near, so that they may be gathered together."
Then, just as he had intended, they all assembled accordingly, and he knew their locations.
At that time, four hundred thousand bhikṣus came and gathered at the vihāra.
The Buddha again addressed the bodhisattva Anabhāsa-lakṣaṇa.
The Bodhisattva Mṛdumati,
the Bodhisattva Sarvodyogaprahīṇa,
and the Bodhisattva Sarvasaumanasyatamovigata.
The Bodhisattva Remover of All Obstructions,
the Bodhisattva Sovereign Lord of All Honored Ones,
and the Bodhisattva Universal Peace whose Voice is Widely Heard and Vision Pervasive.
The Bodhisattva Saugandhika-hasta replied in a single word to the Bodhisattvas of Ten Million Billion Voices,
Maitreya Bodhisattva, and the others.
"Good son, go to the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
call out there to all those who have resolved their minds on Bodhisattvahood—
both those who have attained *avaivartika* status and those who have not."

Those who had already attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and those who had not yet attained it were all made to assemble at the Gabled Hall (*Vimāna*).
Ten bodhisattvas each received the Buddha’s instruction, prostrated themselves, and departed.
It reached everywhere throughout the lands of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
At that time, eight billion hundred thousand bodhisattvas who were in their last birth before Buddhahood (*ekajātipratibaddha*) came to the assembly;
one billion hundred thousand bodhisattvas who were non-retrogressive (*avaivartika*) came to the assembly.
Three billion bodhisattvas who had attained the patience regarding the non-arising of all phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) came to the assembly.
Six billion bodhisattvas with pure resolve and liberation came to the assembly.
Those who had first conceived the great resolve and those who acted in accordance with the Dharma were beyond counting; they were all of one kind, sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power.
Each arrived here from the ten directions,
prostrated before the Buddha, and sat together in assembly.
At that time, Śāriputra observed that the ranks and classes of the bodhisattva multitude differed, and their respective dwellings were not the same.
Then, as those of the same class all flew together to the assembly,
they spoke in alarm and fear, saying,
"This must have been brought about by the merit and supernatural power of the Buddha."
"For what reason have you come to this assembly?
Thereupon, Śāriputra rose from his seat,
paid homage to the Buddha, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
I have a doubt that I now wish to ask the Buddha,
so as to enable the bodhisattvas in this assembly to attain direct faith;
having heard what the Buddha teaches, each may find their own proper place.
May the sūtras and dharmas taught by Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges be heard equally by all, and may they attain purity;
may he be able to answer all the various questions posed by countless people.
By practicing what kind of Dharma-conduct will one never lose one's resolve and swiftly attain the unsurpassed,
equal Way of Supreme Perfect Enlightenment?
The Buddha said, "Excellent, excellent, Śāriputra!
It is indeed for the sake of all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas that you wish to inquire into this meaning; how delightful is this!"
The Buddha said, "Listen attentively, uphold it well, and contemplate it.
I shall provide you with a profound liberation,
so that all who hear it may swiftly attain the unsurpassed, equal Way of Supreme Perfect Enlightenment."
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
“These bodhisattvas, having already attained this dharani-sūtra,
illuminate all dharmas and act as guides for all dharmas.”
Why is this? It is for the sake of worldly people.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
"There are four matters by which a bodhisattva attains this Dharma."
What are the four? First, one is always careful and restrained in bodily conduct.
Second, one is always sincere in verbal expression.
Third, their thoughts are always gentle and compliant.
Fourth, they skillfully employ expedient means to rescue and protect all beings.
These are the four matters.
This is because they employ the correct method.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
"Furthermore, there are four things by which a bodhisattva attains the inexhaustible wisdom of the empty body."
What are the four? First, by means of dwelling in purity,
one burns away all hardships and dissipates the stains of doubt.
First, to deliver all the people of the world;
second, to guide and benefit all by means of pure abiding and the upholding of all sūtras and dharmas;
third, to benefit all through the merits produced by pure abiding.
Fourth, purifying all buddha-fields and enabling all beings to transcend [suffering] so that they attain the Buddha-dharma.
These are the four matters.
The wisdom of the pure abiding of the empty body is inexhaustible.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
"Furthermore, there are four matters by which a bodhisattva maintains the *dhāraṇīmukha* and enters into birth-and-death, thereby swiftly attaining [enlightenment]."
What are the four? First, through the *dhāraṇīmukha*, one causes worldly name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) to quickly attain the pure dharmas.
Second, through the *dhāraṇīmukha*, one enters into patience (*kṣānti*).
Third, the *dhāraṇīmukha* that enters the root of all thoughts and conceptions.
Fourth, the *dhāraṇīmukha* that enters all dharmas of good and evil deeds, causing them to be swiftly attained.
These are the four matters by which one swiftly attains this *dhāraṇīmukha*.
The Buddha said: "If a bodhisattva wishes to attain the *ānandamukha-nirhāra-dhāraṇī*, [they should practice these four]."
One should first understand and awaken to the forty-eight names.
What are these forty-eight? They are: A-kie (Akṣaya), Wu-wei (Asaṃskṛta), and so forth.
Silent restraint is the Samantamukha-pratipatti; through diligent application and discipline,
one attains the tranquility of cessation.
Parābhā-jyoti-īle-anuśāsana-kalpa-nitya-smṛti.
The supreme arts of Kapphina and Śāriputra;
the sublime phrases of Śāradvatīputra.
Heila has mind; Helei is without intention;
Heilile has no thoughts in the mind; Chandri is liberation; Chalanī is the practitioner.
Pho-ca-ni, mi-dong,
a-lan-ni, tha-yu, nye-mud-ti, mi-thod.
Nirvṛti (Nirvana), Anutpāda (Non-arising),
Nirañjana (Stainless), Vimala-caryā (Undefiled Conduct),
Śubha-nirmita (Purely Adorned).
Pārahitabhaṇi, who is free from violence and arrogance,
whose fame has reached Aśvajit.
Dhammika, Anihata, Vimala, Khema, Samādhi, Saṅkha, and Dīghāloka.
Cittī asi citrābhir ūtibhiḥ mahāṃś citraś citrābhir ūtibhiḥ niṣṭigryaḥ pātva ahasaḥ.
(RV 10.99.7) [Nighaṇṭu 3.11] *niṣṭigryaḥ* is a word expressing praise (*praśaṃsā*).
Acchariya (the marvelous),
anacchariya (the non-marvelous),
and samacchariya (the equal marvelous).
Tilottamā, next Kāñcanamālā, Citrā, Gati,
Akṣayamati, and Vighuṣṭaśabda;
these are those who practice unimpeded conduct.
Samantamukha, the Universal Honored One, Nihāra-śuddhi-vīrya-caryā,
Sumeru-Sumeru-dambhita, Vidyā-sthiti-candra-rāja, Dṛḍha-bala-parākrama.
Gomati attains great power;
Mahākāśyapa possesses great radiance;
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra has long-lasting illumination.
Sāhālūnō kēti saṃpariggahe anācikkhiyā anantā dhāraṇī mukha-dvāna-ti nō atthi paccuppanna-buddhena bhāsitā iti imāni aṭṭhacattālīsa nāmāni etassa parittassa.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"A bodhisattva should contemplate the dhāraṇī thus:
whether it be dharmas that are liberated or dharmas that are not liberated."
One does not perform this performance;
one neither knows nor understands it,
and therein nothing is added.
Nor is there any decrease.
One neither perceives liberation nor non-liberation;
one neither perceives arising nor cessation.
One does not perceive the future, the past, or the present;
one does not perceive coming, nor does one perceive going;
one seeks no Buddha, nor does one turn the mind away from it.
Neither are they marks of excellence nor do they plant the seeds of excellence;
neither are they retinues nor do they possess precepts;
neither are they samādhi nor are they wisdom.
Neither is there liberation, nor is there the wisdom that perceives liberation.
There is neither sitting nor walking, nor is there anything to be attained.
There is neither the removal of defilements, nor is there wisdom, nor is there the absence of wisdom.
Neither does one instruct, nor does one purify anything;
there is neither self nor person;
there is neither dharma nor diligence.
It is neither practiced nor purified;
it is neither body, nor mind, nor speech;
it does not belong to the future, nor the past, nor the present; it is not for one's own sake, nor for the sake of another's body.
Thus, Śāriputra, this Dharma is called the unsurpassed and most supreme Dharma among all dharmas;
it also gathers and compiles all dharmas.
It also enters into all dharmas;
this is called mindfulness of all Buddha-dharmas.
This dharani is named "The Fierce One of Dharma."
Briefly summarizing all phenomena,
this is called the "Chapter on Clear Understanding.
It purifies all people and fulfills their aspirations.
This causes one to attain the samādhi of renown and awakening;
this is called the complete fulfillment of one's own fundamental merit.
This is called the accumulation of the seeds of Dharma and the activation of all mental faculties.
They cause him to be deeply honored, adorned with the marks and signs of excellence such that none can move him;
even if celestial Māras come, they cannot destroy him;
none can seize him, and none can approach him.

In this way, Śāriputra, any bodhisattva who hears this *ānandamukha-nirhāra-dhāraṇī* shall be considered to have already attained the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*) and the path of supreme equanimity.
Why is this? Because regarding the conduct of all Buddhas, they have already fully perfected it and act for the sake of all beings;
they destroy the cycle of birth and death within the five realms of existence as well as all fetters of doubt.
May they quickly attain dharani.
At that time, the Buddha spoke these verses:
"Do not harbor thoughts of 'empty dharmas,' And do not speak lightly of 'attainment' or 'non-attainment.'"
Believe directly in the Dharma and do not harbor doubts within; then you will swiftly attain *dhāraṇī*.
Fearing that you might be bound by this emptiness, analyze emptiness to quickly attain Buddhahood.
This essential wisdom is boundless and bottomless; one will swiftly and closely attain *dhāraṇī*.
The Bodhisattva upholds the dhāraṇī, which universally encompasses all dharmas;
by hearing the teachings of the Buddhas of the ten directions,
they fully attain the wisdom of the *dhāraṇī-nigama-dhāraṇī*, which is like the great radiance of the sun.
The Dharma of the Prediction upon Receiving the Names of All Buddhas:
Purely upholding it, one attains the realization of the Dharma; this is the *mukha-dhāraṇī*.
Whatever exists that manifests before one, among all dharmas it is the most supreme; It universally protects and guards all people in the world.
May they cause humans and non-humans throughout the ten directions, for the duration of an eon, to ask about the meaning of wisdom;

may they resolve all their doubts. When that eon has ended, their knowledge shall not be exhausted, provided they receive and trust in the path of the sutras, and with diligence uphold the Middle Way of the True Dharma.
One who is close to being reborn to fill that place shall immediately become a Dharma Prince.
If one upholds this dhāraṇī, one will be pitied by all people,
one’s fame will pervade Jambudvīpa, and one will be praised by the World-Honored One.
Those who uphold this sutra shall, at the time of their death,
all behold eight billion koṭis of buddhas extending their hands to bestow upon them rebirth in a noble place;
those who train in this dhāraṇī shall do so throughout the course of ten trillion kalpas.
Whatever evil deeds and delusions one has committed will all be extinguished within a single month;
yet if a bodhisattva performs meritorious acts of giving for ten billion kalpas without weariness, it would not equal the virtue attained by studying the dhāraṇī for one month.
The merit of the latter remains equal [to the former] throughout that month.
Having fully received and expounded the *dhāraṇī*, and having attained all samādhis and wisdom, one’s mind becomes irreversible;
such a person shall attain Buddhahood, possess a buddha-field, and receive offerings.
Those who uphold this sutra shall cause even those in the three realms to act as Māras.
Desires may seek to disturb and destroy their minds, yet they can never shake them;
having fully realized that all things are empty, they give rise to countless Buddhas.
Such words are no different from this: the *dhāraṇī* is inexhaustible.
Hearing these matters in this place, Dīrghanakha received my prediction that he would become Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; at that time,
he immediately perceived the Truths and upheld this sutra scroll, whereby all his vows were swiftly fulfilled.
The Method for Entering the Buddha-lands: According to what is appropriate, one is able to transform and deliver beings, constantly purifying the Buddha-lands;
Being without blemish among the Saṃgha, one asks about the profound and subtle Dharma; One is able to fully know all such volumes of this sutra.
He is entirely free from lustful indulgence; regarding thought, he possesses the seven factors of enlightenment.
He upholds eighty billion Buddhas and others through dhāraṇīs, always abiding with a mind that does not dwell on what is improper.
One should not think of it; be careful not to think of it at all.
Thus one should maintain mindfulness and never lose it;
later, having attained immeasurable merit, one should always understand the matters of this sutra.
Be careful not to harbor any doubt, for it is like a person who has entered the great ocean and would never say that the jewels are difficult to find.
They shall experience the bliss of devas and humans endowed with merit;
such a state will not be far off, and they shall also swiftly attain Buddhahood. For this reason, Śāriputra, do not be separated from the Buddha.
The Buddha told Śāriputra: "There are four practices for a bodhisattva."
One will swiftly attain the dhāraṇī method.
What are the four? First, to remain far removed from worldly desire and lust.
Second, one does not speak of the long and short of others, so that others find no opportunity for harm.
Third, when someone comes to request something, one does not oppose their wishes;
giving without any sense of attachment or stinginess, one later feels no regret.
Fourth, to practice with diligence day and night, always intent on seeking all dharmas.
These are the four matters.
Śāriputra, the bodhisattva practices these.
One will swiftly attain *dhāraṇī*.
At that time, the Buddha spoke these verses:
"Those who distance themselves from all evils and depart from sensual desire, yet commit sinful deeds, shall fall into hell."
Free from the calamities of the three poisons, they do not give rise to them; having renounced what is loved, they obtain this sutra.
They do not envy others, nor do they boast of their own kin;
they always maintain an impartial mind toward all beings. Their physical bodies are exceedingly upright and handsome.
Constantly renouncing what the body delights in, being without anger or strife toward the world,
and not engaging in worldly affairs, one shall soon attain the *dhāraṇī*;
by studying with constant diligence day and night, one has no expectations for non-Buddhist paths.
One should seek the supreme Dharma in this way; the *dhāraṇī* will manifest spontaneously.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
"A bodhisattva has four practices."
One will swiftly attain this dharani. What are the four?
First, dwelling alone in a secluded place.
Second, abiding in the profound patience of the Dharma (*gambhīradharmanidhyānakṣānti*). Third, not being delighted by offerings or gifts.
Fourth, not cherishing one’s own body or life.
How much more so with wealth and treasures.
Śāriputra, these are the four matters by which a bodhisattva who practices them will swiftly attain [enlightenment].
At that time, the Tathāgata spoke these verses:
"Abiding in solitude, one should contemplate the True Dharma; One should not treat others with contempt.
The realm of birth and death is like wearing a torch upon one's head; Having obtained this human body, one must practice accordingly."
Always maintaining the mind in profound patience, being content with wealth and treasures, and remaining seated in the noble lineage with an impartial mind;
not showing partiality toward one's own clan, but solely making offerings to the Buddha and the Dharma;
abiding in the power of goodness, one transcends the hardships of the world.
One who immediately alters their appearance and shaves off beard and hair shall thereby attain virtue and enter the subtle and wondrous;

one should know both emptiness and worldly affairs. For this reason, the foolish practitioner abandons all possessions, yet remains greedy for wealth and profit, lacking in precepts, patience, and wisdom.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra,
"Furthermore, there are four practices by which a bodhisattva will swiftly attain this dhāraṇī."
What are the four? First,
there are eight categories of syllables that open the way into wisdom, understanding, and discernment.
What are these eight? The first is called *pā*.
It causes all phenomena characterized by attachment to enter into the dharma of emptiness.
The second is called *la*.
Whether the Tathāgata manifests the marks and signs of physical excellence or does not manifest them,
he enters into all phenomena by means of the Dharma-body.
The third is called *ba* (va),
which refers to the deluded phenomena (*moha-dharma*) and the wise phenomena (*prajñā-dharma*) that cause one to enter into the understanding of the Dharma of wisdom (*prajñā*).
The fourth is called *jia* (ka).
To know the destinations to which various calamities and transgressions lead, and cause them to enter into merit and blessings—
this is called *ja*. To know birth,
old age, sickness, and death, and thereby immediately enter into the formless (*ārūpya*)— this is the fifth.
The sixth is called *dhā* (Dhāraṇī):
viewing all lands and the world as empty, one enters into wishlessness (*apraṇihita*) without being startled or amazed.
The seventh is called *śa* (Śamatha).
To bring all phenomena to rest and cause them to enter the state of coolness is called the eighth, *aṣṭama*.
To know that all phenomena are empty is the eighth.
Furthermore, there are four matters:
first, to constantly contemplate the eight characters;
second, if one writes this sutra, one should write it with careful attention.
Third, if one upholds this sutra, one should uphold it with earnest attention and recite it until the fifteenth day.
Fourth, one should practice according to the Dharma and contemplate the eight characters.
These are the four matters.
Śāriputra, by practicing in this way,
a bodhisattva quickly attains dhāraṇī.
At that time, the Buddha spoke these verses:
One should always keep in mind these eight characters; Transcribe them, uphold this scroll, and practice them with earnest devotion.
Read them on the fifteenth day and never depart from them. Exhort all to seek the path of the Buddha;
one must learn to transform and enlighten others. Thus one shall swiftly attain wisdom and draw near to Buddhahood.
He sees all the Buddhas of the ten directions, as if they were all standing before him.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
"Furthermore, there are four things for a bodhisattva."
By recollecting the dhāraṇī, one attains the benefits of the Dharma. What are these four?
First, one is constantly recollected by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, of the ten directions.
Second, in whatever they undertake, Māra cannot destroy their resolve.
Third, all karmic offenses from past lives are completely extinguished.
Fourth, they never cease speaking with utmost sincerity, and are able to provide definitive answers to all questions.
These are the four matters.
Śāriputra, these are the benefits of a bodhisattva attaining the dharma of dhāraṇī.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
They are constantly kept in mind by all Buddhas; Māra cannot find an opportunity against them, and the sins they have committed are immediately extinguished. They are liberated from all doubts.
Thus spoke the Buddha to Śāriputra.
In the past, throughout ages as incalculable as they have passed,
and even many times more— so vast, so long, and so beyond measure that they can no longer be reckoned—
there was at that time a Buddha in the world.
He was named Tathāgata King Endowed with Jewels and Virtuous Conduct.
Having transcended the four paths and not receiving the peace of perfect enlightenment,
he was established in the heavens as the God among Gods.
That Buddha preached the Dharma for all beings such that none could surpass him.
When he was about to enter parinirvāṇa, there was a golden-wheel-turning monarch named Dhara who ruled over the four continents; his son’s name was Amanasikāra.
Endowed with a full reputation and sixteen years of age,
the prince then went to the place where the Buddha was and heard that Buddha preach the *Dhāraṇī Sūtra*.
Having heard it, he rejoiced and immediately obtained this sutra.
Having obtained it, he recited and studied it, constantly mindful of upholding it.
For seven thousand years, he practiced with such diligence that he did not sleep and his side never rested upon a mat.
For seven thousand years he did not think of sensual desires;
for seven thousand years he did not think of wealth and treasures;
for seven thousand years he did not inquire about other matters.
For seven thousand years, he constantly dwelt alone, his mind remaining unshaken;
at that time, he heard ninety-nine billion incalculable Buddhas preaching the Dharma of wisdom, and having heard it, [he attained realization].
He then abandoned his kingdom and renounced his kingship to become a śramaṇa.
For ninety-nine thousand years, he practiced the Ānanda-mukha-nigama-dhāraṇī and further expounded it to all beings.
In a single lifetime, he transformed the people of the world,
causing eight hundred million nayutas of beings to all resolve their minds upon the unsurpassed, impartial path.
Upon attaining the stage of *avaivartika*,
there was then a son of a householder named Candrarāja who heard this *dhāraṇī* within the great assembly.
Having heard this, they encourage others to uphold it.
Through the merit of this encouragement and rejoicing, they reach ninety million billion buddha-fields,
making offerings to all Buddhas and establishing meritorious roots.
In all those Buddha-lands, they shall attain all *dhāraṇīs* and immediately reach the stage of being "born only once more" (*ekajātipratibaddha*),
becoming flying bodhisattvas.
The Buddha spoke to the bodhisattvas:
"During these three kalpas, you shall make offerings to that many Buddhas.
Once the three kalpas have passed, you shall attain the unsurpassed, equal path of supreme perfect enlightenment."
At that time, the elder’s son Candrarāja was none other than the Buddha Dīpaṃkara;
and the king Dhāraṇīputra, named Anantanirghoṣa, was none other than Amitābha Buddha.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
"During the Bhadrakalpa,
I have taught the dhāraṇīs to the various bodhisattvas."
Those who, upon hearing this sutra, experience sympathetic joy and thereby exhort all others,
perform acts of giving that assist and promote merit.
Having transcended four hundred thousand kalpas, they will no longer undergo toil and suffering;
thereafter, they shall attain the Way and act with full autonomy of mind.
Furthermore, after having made offerings to nine hundred billion buddhas, they shall likewise attain this.
One shall attain the unsurpassed, equal path of supreme perfect enlightenment.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
"If there is a bodhisattva who, at the very last, hears this dhāraṇī..."
The merit of one who upholds, encourages, and rejoices in [the practice] is such as this.
If there is a bodhisattva who, by virtue of the merit of rejoicing, [attains...]
If, through a mind of loving-kindness, one sheds tears and the hair on one's body stands on end upon hearing this sutra,
all such persons shall attain the unsurpassed path of equality and be led into the stage of *avaivartika*.
Śāriputra, if one takes up, studies, recites, chants, or reads such skillful means texts,
the merit of those people is immeasurable, incomparable, and unspeakable.
No sentient beings are able to calculate or fathom its limit.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"If one hears this and further encourages others to assist, And writes it down, upholds it, recites it, and reads it,"
The devas and humans may calculate his virtue, yet none can know the limit of his blessings;

wherever he is born, he constantly beholds the Buddha. Having attained the realization of wisdom through the profound sutras, he firmly upholds the Dharma, immovable by any power; thus he swiftly attains clear understanding and awakening.
Always with a concentrated mind, neither increasing nor decreasing, Truly attaining the *dhāraṇī* without loss,
and establishing the marks and signs while free from the perception of form, He becomes a peerless Hero of the World;
when the son of a householder hears this sutra, In every place of birth, he shall know his past lives.
One will always behold countless honored ones; Just as one wishes, one shall immediately attain Buddhahood.

If one desires to quickly attain Buddhahood, And swiftly depart from all demons, Or if one desires to obtain the hundred marks of merit, By constantly recollecting this, one shall attain it before long.
"Even if one were to fill as many Buddha-fields as there are grains of sand in the Ganges with precious jewels and offer them as a gift,
it would not equal the merit of one who writes out and upholds this [sūtra]. Śāriputra, this analogy is exactly as the Buddha has spoken."
If there is a bodhisattva who maintains mindfulness and studies the dhāraṇī,
there is a mountain named Himavān where eight spirits reside;
they constantly protect such a person and open their mind and will.
What are the eight?
First is the spirit named Brave and Powerful;
second is the spirit named Illuminating the Ten Directions.
The third was named Beneficial-to-Many Ghost-King;
the fourth was named Great-Power Dragon-King Ghost-King;
the fifth was named Sincere-Practice Ghost-King.
Sixth is the spirit named Able-to-Tame-the-Untamed;
seventh is the spirit named Youthful Male;
eighth is the spirit named Swift-Arm.
These are the names of the eight deities.
If one studies this sutra and wishes to cause the deities to come,
one should purify oneself by bathing and washing, and put on new clothes.
When walking in meditation, one should always maintain a mind of loving-kindness toward all beings; having first composed the mind,
one should recite the dhāraṇī, upholding this sūtra with firm devotion.
Then, their delusions were swiftly dispelled and they attained wisdom.
At that moment, the spirits stood before him.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
Furthermore, there are eight bodhisattvas dwelling in the heavens of the desire realm who constantly and impartially protect the people and bestow upon them the Way of the sutras.
Who are these eight?
The first was named Devaputra Illuminating the Ten Directions;
the second was named Devaputra World-Knower;
the third was named Devaputra Wisdom-Light.
The fourth is named Sunlight Devaputra;
the fifth is named Superior Examination Devaputra;
the sixth is named Fulfiller of Wishes Devaputra.
The seventh is named Nakṣatrarājadevaputra;
the eighth is named Caritramatidevaputra.
These are the names of the eight devaputras.
Constantly and impartially protect the people and exhort those who uphold this sutra to maintain mindfulness,
so that they may quickly attain concentration and obtain dharanis.
Those who seek this sutra should always apply themselves with diligence and mindfulness to the teachings on dharanis.
One should practice a single dharma without deficiency regarding the sutras and precepts;
what one speaks must be sincere, and one’s conduct should be likewise.
One should always be filial and obedient toward all those who are venerable.
Regard all people as no different from the Buddha;
do not treat those whom you hold dear with a disrespectful mind.
Constantly reflect upon the principle of reciprocity, and you will immediately obtain a favorable retribution.
He then attained profound patience (*kṣānti*) and gained the vision of the dharma of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma*).
When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra,
bodhisattvas equal in number to the sands of thirty-two Ganges Rivers all attained *dhāraṇī* and established themselves on the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika-bhūmi*).
Six billion devaputras attained the patience regarding the non-arising of all phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Thirty-two thousand gods and humans conceived the aspiration for the unsurpassed, equal Way.
At that time, the trichiliocosm shook in six ways.
Heavenly flowers rained down, and lutes and musical instruments resounded spontaneously without being struck.
Then Śāriputra stepped forward and asked the Buddha,
"World-Honored One, what is the name of this sutra, and how should it be practiced?"
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
"This sūtra is named Ānandamukhanirhāradharani;
it swiftly enables sentient beings to attain all-knowledge."
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra,
Śāriputra, as well as the countless bodhisattvas of the ten directions,
devas, humans, gandharvas, asuras, and world-protectors, [all rejoiced].
They all rejoiced, approached, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, paid their respects, and departed.
This concludes the *Ānandamukha-nīhārita-dhāraṇī-sūtra* spoken by the Buddha.
